title: Chapter 1: Command Line Basics

Chapter 1: Command Line Basics

🏛️ Command Line Launching & Syntax

* 🖥️ **Default Boot Interface:** By default, 🪟 Windows boots into a graphical user interface (GUI).
* 🚨 **System Diagnostics:** If 🪟 Windows boots into something other than the default graphical interface (or one of the versions of Safe Mode), you can assume that something has gone wrong with your system.
* 💡 **Terminal Access:** You type lines of text in the terminal which the command interpreter (CMD.EXE) converts into instruction sets.

<CommandLineBasicsSimulation />

Every command in ⊞ Windows follows this standard structure:

COMMAND [arguments]

* **Command:** The action you want to perform (e.g. `ver` to check version, or `cls` to clear screen).
* **Arguments:** Extra specifications that tell the command *where* or *how* to act (e.g. `help dir`).

Basic Shell Commands:
* **`ver`**: Prints your operating system build name.
* **`help [command]`**: Accesses the built-in instruction manual for any command.
* **`cls`**: Clears the console screen of all past text clutter.

🖥️ Making the Command Prompt Window Larger

By default, the ⊞ Windows Command Prompt window is not very large. Even if you click the standard **maximize** button, the window will typically not expand to take up more than about a third of your screen space.

To resize and customize the window layout:
1. 🖱️ **Open Properties:** Right-click on the Command Prompt window's top **title bar**, and select **Properties** from the context menu.
2. 🎚️ **Navigate to Layout:** When the Properties dialog window opens, click on the **Layout Tab**.
3. 📏 **Adjust Window Size:** Under the *Window Size* section, you can manually adjust the **Width** and **Height** values (in character units) to expand the default terminal dimensions. Click **OK** to apply!

> [!TIP]
> **Modern Terminal Alternative:**
> In 🪟 Windows 11, you can also use the new **Windows Terminal** app, which supports standard full-screen maximization, tabs, and zoom scaling (`Ctrl` + `+` / `Ctrl` + `-`) out-of-the-box! 🚀

title: Chapter 2: Drive Letters and the File System

Chapter 2: Drive Letters and the File System

💾 Storage Drives & Volume Layouts

Unlike Unix-based operating systems (like macOS or Linux) which merge all storage drives into a single root directory (`/`), 🪟 Windows organizes storage partitions using alphabetical letters followed by a colon:
* **`C:`**: The primary local drive (where the 🪟 Windows 11 system files and operating system are installed).
* **`D:`**: The secondary drive (often used for data backups, extra software, or USB storage).
* **`F:`**: Shared network drives or virtual mounted partitions.

Every drive has its own independent root directory represented by a backslash `\`. For example, `C:\` represents the root directory of the C drive.

title: Chapter 3: Understanding the Prompt
content:
Chapter 3: Understanding the Prompt

⚡ Customizing the Command Prompt

The text indicator to the left of your cursor is called the **prompt**. It usually shows your active folder path, but did you know you can customize it using the `prompt` command?

By typing `prompt` followed by a text string, you change your prompt indicator:

C:\Users\Student> prompt Student$
Student$


To restore the default prompt displaying your current directory path, simply run:

Student$ prompt
C:\Users\Student>


---

🎨 Special Prompt Codes

You can use special dollar-sign `$` codes to display dynamic system information in the prompt:

| Code | Output Content | Example Output |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`$P`** | Current drive and folder path | `C:\Users\Student` |
| **`$G`** | The greater-than angle bracket `>` | `>` |
| **`$D`** | Current system date | `Mon 07/06/2026` |
| **`$T`** | Current system time | `23:45:12.84` |
| **`$V`** | 🪟 Windows version number | `Microsoft Windows [Version 10.0.22621.1702]` |
| **`$S`** | A space character | |
| **`$$`** | A literal dollar sign `$` | `$` |

Creating the Default Prompt:
The standard prompt you see is generated by the combination of `$P` (current path) and `$G` (greater-than bracket):

prompt $P$G


---

🎨 Changing Terminal Colors and Window Title

🌈 The `color` Command
You can change the background and text color of your command window using the `color` command followed by a two-character hex code (first character for background, second for text):

color 0A

* `0` = Black background
* `A` = Light Green text (classic matrix style!)

Common color codes include:
* `0` = Black, `1` = Blue, `2` = Green, `3` = Aqua, `4` = Red, `5` = Purple, `6` = Yellow, `7` = White, `8` = Gray, `9` = Light Blue
* `A` = Light Green, `B` = Light Aqua, `C` = Light Red, `D` = Light Purple, `E` = Light Yellow, `F` = Bright White

🏷️ The `title` Command
To change the title bar name of the Command Prompt window, use `title` followed by your custom name:

title Nextsem Academy Terminal

title: Chapter 4: Working with Directories
content:
Chapter 4: Working with Directories

📂 Managing Directories & Navigation

Managing directories (folders) without a mouse is one of the most fundamental skills in 🪟 Windows 11 system administration.

* **`mkdir [name]`** (or `md`): Creates a new folder. Remember the **Zero-Space Rule** (use hyphens like `Week-1` instead of spaces).
* **`cd [folder]`**: Steps inside a specific folder (relative path navigation).
* **`cd ..`**: Moves backward one step to the parent directory.
* **`cd \`**: Jumps all the way back to the root directory of the active drive.

---

🔍 Advanced Directory Audits with `dir`

The `dir` command list files and folders, but you can refine its output using switches:

| Switch | Action | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`/P`** | Pauses output page-by-page (useful for very large folders). | `dir /p` |
| **`/W`** | Lists directories in a wide multi-column layout. | `dir /w` |
| **`/A`** | Filters files by specific attributes: | |
| | * `/AD`: Lists **directories only** (hides files). | `dir /ad` |
| | * `/AH`: Lists **hidden files only**. | `dir /ah` |
| **`/O`** | Sorts files (e.g. `/ON` sorts by name, `/OS` sorts by size). | `dir /os` |
| **`/S`** | Searches the current directory and all subdirectories for matching files. | `dir *.txt /s` |

---

🧹 Deleting Directories with `rmdir` (or `rd`)

To remove a directory, use the `rmdir` command:

rmdir Nextsem


> [!WARNING]
> **Directory Not Empty:**
> By default, `rmdir` will fail if the folder contains any files or other folders!

To force-delete a folder and all of its contents (subfolders and files) recursively, you must use the `/s` (subdirectories) switch:

rmdir Nextsem /s

title: Chapter 5: File Attributes and NTFS Permissions
content:
Chapter 5: File Attributes and NTFS Permissions

🔒 File Attributes & The Attrib Command

In 🪟 Windows, every file has properties called **attributes** that dictate how the OS displays, logs, and protects them:
* 🔒 **Read-Only (`R`):** Locks the file, preventing editing, writing, or deletion.
* 👻 **Hidden (`H`):** Hides the file from standard file viewer lists and basic `dir` queries.
* ⚙️ **System (`S`):** Identifies the file as an operating system file that cannot be moved or deleted.
* 📦 **Archive (`A`):** Marks the file for backup (is checked by backup utilities to see if it changed since the last copy).

You configure these using the **`attrib`** command:
* ➕🔑 **`attrib +r [filename]`**: Locks the file as **Read-Only** (gives it the `R` tag).
* ➕👻 **`attrib +h [filename]`**: **Hides** the file.
* ➕⚙️ **`attrib +s [filename]`**: Marks it as a **System** file.

> 🔒 **Access Blocked:** If a file is locked as Read-Only, trying to run `del filename` will trigger a system-level `Access is denied` block!

---

🔑 NTFS Permissions (Security ACLs)

While attributes apply basic rules to a file, **NTFS permissions** allow fine-grained access controls matching specific users or groups:

* **Full Control (`F`):** Can read, write, edit, delete, and alter security permissions.
* **Modify (`M`):** Can read, write, and delete files, but cannot change ownership/permissions.
* **Read & Execute (`RX`):** Can open, view, and run application files.
* **Read (`R`):** Can view file contents only.
* **Write (`W`):** Can write to or append file data.

Inheritance vs Explicit Permissions
* **Inherited Permissions:** Permissions passed down from parent folders (e.g. if you have full control over `C:\Users\Student`, you inherit full control over its subfolders).
* **Explicit Permissions:** Permissions directly assigned to a specific file or folder, overriding parent folder settings.

---

🛡️ Modifying Access Lists with `icacls`

To display, modify, or backup file and folder access lists, 🪟 Windows uses the **`icacls`** command:

🔎 Displaying Permissions:

icacls config.txt

*Outputs current access control entries (ACEs), showing which users (e.g. Administrators, Users, SYSTEM) have what access shorthand (`(I)` = Inherited, `(F)` = Full Control).*

➕ Granting User Permissions:
To grant a user modified access:

icacls config.txt /grant Student:M


❌ Denying User Permissions:
To explicitly block a user:

icacls config.txt /deny Administrator:F

title: Chapter 6: Wildcards and Redirection
content:
Chapter 6: Wildcards and Redirection

🌟 Wildcards: The * and ? Filters

Wildcards are placeholder symbols used to select groups of files matching a specific pattern:

* **`*` (Asterisk):** Matches **any number of characters** (including zero).
  * `*.html` matches `index.html`, `main.html`, etc.
  * `project*` matches `project1.zip`, `project-final.doc`, etc.
  * `*.*` matches **every file** in the directory.
* **`?` (Question Mark):** Matches **exactly one character**.
  * `logo?.png` matches `logo1.png`, `logoA.png`, but *not* `logo12.png`.
  * `file??.txt` matches `file01.txt`, `fileAB.txt`, but *not* `file1.txt`.

---

➡️ Redirection: Command Output Controls

By default, 🪟 Windows sends command outputs to the screen. You can redirect this stream using the following operators:

* **`>` (Overwrite Redirect):** Directs output to a file, overwriting the file if it already exists.
  * `dir > folder-log.txt` (saves the active folder structure to a text file).
* **`>>` (Append Redirect):** Appends output to the end of a file without deleting its current contents.
  * `echo Server Online >> status.log` (adds a log line to an existing status file).
* **`<` (Input Redirect):** Feeds a file's content *into* a command as input.

---

🔗 The Pipe Operator & The `more` Command

🚰 The Pipe Operator (`|`)
The pipe operator takes the output of one command and feeds it directly as the input to a second command:

COMMAND_A | COMMAND_B


📄 The `more` Command
When a folder has hundreds of files, running `dir` scrolls past so fast you cannot read it. You can pipe `dir` into the **`more`** command to display the output page-by-page:

dir | more

* Press **`Spacebar`** to scroll to the next full page.
* Press **`Enter`** to scroll down line-by-line.
* Press **`Q`** to quit the viewer.

> 📝 **Developer Joke:** Why did the console output get redirected to a file? Because it wanted to save its thoughts for later instead of just speaking them to the wall! 🗣️📄

title: Chapter 7: Copying, Moving, Renaming, and Deleting Files
content:
Chapter 7: Copying, Moving, Renaming, and Deleting Files

📄 File Manipulation Operations

Managing system records at the command line requires familiarity with the primary file operations:

* 📑 **`copy [source] [destination]`**: Duplicates a file to a new name or directory path.
* 📦 **`move [source] [destination]`**: Moves a file from its current path to another folder, or renames a directory.
* 🏷️ **`ren [oldname] [newname]`**: Renames a file or folder (short for *rename*).
* 🗑️ **`del [filename]`** (or `erase`): Deletes files.
* 📄 **`type [filename]`**: Displays the text content of a file on-screen.

---

🛠️ Advanced Operation Switches

For bulk automation, these commands support powerful parameters to control behavior and prompt prompts:

Overwriting Confirmation Controls (`/Y`)
By default, if you copy or move a file to a destination where a file with the same name already exists, 🪟 Windows asks if you want to overwrite it.
* **`/Y`**: Suppresses the prompt, automatically overwriting any existing files.
* **`/-Y`**: Explicitly forces the confirmation prompt.


copy /Y index.html backup.html


Force Deleting Read-Only Files (`/F` and `/S` in `del`)
By default, the `del` command fails with `"Access is denied"` if a file is marked with the Read-Only (+r) attribute.
* **`/F`**: Forces deletion of read-only files.
* **`/S`**: Deletes specified files from the current folder and all subdirectories.
* **`/Q`**: Runs in quiet mode (does not prompt you before deleting wildcards).


del /f /s /q test-logs\*.log


---

📂 Bulk Folder Duplication with `xcopy`

The standard `copy` command only duplicates *individual files*, not folders. To copy folders, subfolders, and all contained files, use **`xcopy`**:

* **`/S`**: Copies directories and subdirectories, *excluding* empty ones.
* **`/E`**: Copies directories and subdirectories, *including* empty ones.
* **`/Y`**: Suppresses prompts to overwrite files.


xcopy Nextsem Backups\Nextsem-Backup /E /Y

title: Chapter 8: Networking
content:
Chapter 8: Networking

🌐 Network Configuration & Diagnostics

Troubleshooting network connectivity and configuring interfaces in 🪟 Windows 11 is handled by a set of command-line tools:

📡 The `ipconfig` Command
Displays active network adapter IP details.
* **`ipconfig /all`**: Lists full configuration info including DHCP leases, DNS servers, and MAC address.
* **`ipconfig /flushdns`**: Purges the local DNS resolver cache (crucial when a website changes IPs and you are stuck seeing the old cached site!).
* **`ipconfig /release`** & **`ipconfig /renew`**: Releases and requests a new IP address from the DHCP server.

⚡ The `ping` Command
Sends ICMP Echo Requests to verify a remote server's availability and latency:
* **`ping -t [address]`**: Pings the target host continuously (press `Ctrl` + `C` to stop and view statistics).
* **`ping -n 10 [address]`**: Pings the address exactly 10 times.
* **`ping -a [IP]`**: Attempts to resolve the IP address to a computer hostname.

---

🧭 Advanced Route Tracing & Domain Lookups

🗺️ The `tracert` Command
Traces the route packets take to reach a destination host, showing every intermediate router (hop) and transition latency:

tracert nextsem.online

*Useful for finding exactly where a network connection is failing or which router is causing lag.*

🔍 The `nslookup` Command
Queries the Domain Name System (DNS) server to find the IP address mapping for a domain or check active nameservers:

nslookup nextsem.online


---

🔍 Network Audits: Ports, MACs, & Netsh

🔌 The `netstat` Command
Displays active network connections, routing tables, and port states:
* **`netstat -a`**: Displays all active TCP connections and listening UDP/TCP ports.
* **`netstat -n`**: Shows addresses and port numbers numerically (faster since it skips name lookups).

🏷️ The `getmac` Command
Quickly lists the Media Access Control (MAC) physical addresses of all network adapters on your device.

⚙️ The `netsh` Command
**Network Shell** is a command-line scripting utility that lets you display or modify the network configuration of a computer (e.g. configuring static IPs, modifying 🪟 Windows Defender Firewall rules).

> 💔 **Developer Joke:** Why did the local computer break up with the remote server? It said: "I've been pinging you for hours, but you're giving me nothing but high latency!" 🌐💥

title: Chapter 9: Disk Management
content:
Chapter 9: Disk Management

🛠️ Disk Health Analysis & Auditing

System administrators use dedicated CLI tools to check file system integrity, retrieve storage tags, and manage physical storage volumes in 🪟 Windows 11.

💾 The `vol` Command
Retrieves the volume disk label (name) and the 8-character Volume Serial Number of the active partition:

vol

*Outputs: `Volume in drive C has no label.` and `Volume Serial Number is A4B2-79F8`.*

⚙️ The `chkdsk` Command
The **Check Disk** utility scans filesystem metadata for corruptions and disk sector errors:
* **`chkdsk`**: Runs a read-only scan of the current partition.
* **`chkdsk /f`**: Fixes file system index structure errors on the disk.
* **`chkdsk /r`**: Locates physical bad sectors on the drive and recovers readable text/data (implies `/f`).

---

💿 Advanced Partitioning with `diskpart`

The **Disk Partition Utility (`diskpart`)** is a powerful command-line tool used to configure drives, format partitions, and assign drive letters.

To launch the utility, run:

diskpart

*(Requires administrative privileges. The prompt changes to `DISKPART>` indicating you are inside the interactive partitioning shell).*


graph TD
    dp["DISKPART Shell"] --> ld["list disk"]
    ld --> sd["select disk 0"]
    sd --> lv["list volume"]
    lv --> sv["select volume 2"]
    sv --> fmt["format fs=ntfs quick"]
    fmt --> al["assign letter=D"]
    
    style dp fill:#1e293b,stroke:#3b82f6,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff


Essential `diskpart` Commands:
1. **`list disk`**: Lists all physical storage drives connected to the system.
2. **`select disk [number]`**: Focuses the utility on a specific disk (e.g. `select disk 0`).
3. **`list volume`** / **`list partition`**: Displays active volumes and formatting.
4. **`select volume [number]`**: Selects the target partition (e.g. `select volume 2`).
5. **`clean`**: Erases all partition tables and data from the selected disk.
6. **`create partition primary`**: Allocates raw unallocated space as a primary bootable partition.
7. **`format fs=ntfs quick`**: Formats the selected partition using the **NTFS** filesystem layout.
8. **`assign letter=D`**: Maps the partition to an active drive letter (so it appears in File Explorer).
9. **`exit`**: Exits the `diskpart` shell back to standard CMD.

> [!CAUTION]
> **Data Loss Risk:**
> Running the `clean` command inside `diskpart` instantly deletes all partition layouts on the selected disk! Always verify which disk is selected using `list disk` before executing.

> 🔊 **Developer Joke:** Why was the disk volume always so loud? Because it had a very high volume disk label! 💾🔊

title: Chapter 10: Connecting to File Shares
content:
Chapter 10: Connecting to File Shares

📁 Mounting Network File Shares with `net use`

In professional network environments, shared directories are hosted on central file servers. You can map (mount) these paths to a virtual drive letter on your PC using the **`net use`** command:


net use Z: \\central-server\shared-docs

*This mounts the shared `shared-docs` directory from `central-server` onto the `Z:` drive letter, making it instantly accessible in 🪟 Windows File Explorer.*

Shorthand & Custom Arguments:
* **View Active Connections:** Running **`net use`** without arguments lists all active network mappings, connection status, and drive letters.
* **Persistent Connections:** By default, mapped drives disconnect when you log out. To make them permanent (survive reboots), add `/persistent:yes`:
  
  net use Z: \\central-server\shared-docs /persistent:yes
  
* **Authenticating with Credentials:** If the share requires security authentication, supply credentials inline:
  
  net use Z: \\central-server\shared-docs secretPassword /user:Student
  
* **Disconnecting a Mapped Share:**
  
  net use Z: /delete
  

---

🔎 Auditing Shares with `net view` & `net share`

🌐 Listing Network Shares (`net view`)
To see what folders are shared on a remote computer, use the **`net view`** command:

net view \\central-server

*Displays a list of all shared resource names (like printers and directories) hosted on that IP or server.*

🛠️ Creating Local Shares (`net share`)
You can share your own folders with other users on your local area network (LAN) using the **`net share`** utility:
* **Create a Share:**
  
  net share ProjectWork=C:\Users\Student\Desktop\Nextsem
  
  *This shares the local folder `Nextsem` on the network under the alias `ProjectWork`.*
* **Delete a Share:**
  
  net share ProjectWork /delete
  

> 🔗 **Developer Joke:** Why did the drive letter mount the file share? Because it wanted to stay connected in a long-distance relationship! 🔗📁

title: Chapter 11: Managing User Accounts
content:
Chapter 11: Managing User Accounts

👥 Managing System Profiles with `net user`

In 🪟 Windows 11, system administrators use the **`net user`** command to manage local accounts, enforce security policies, and configure access permissions:

* **List Accounts:** Running **`net user`** without arguments lists all user profiles registered on the computer (e.g. Administrator, Guest, Student).
* **View Account Details:**
  
  net user Student
  
  *Displays detailed info for `Student`, such as password expiry, last login time, and group memberships.*

---

➕ Creating & Configuring User Accounts

👤 Adding a New User
To register a new local user with a defined password:

net user coder nextsem123 /add

If you want to enter the password securely (hidden from shoulder-surfers), use an asterisk `*`:

net user coder * /add

*(The shell will prompt you to type and confirm the password without displaying characters on-screen).*

🛠️ Enforcing Security Constraints & Options
You can configure strict login limits using inline switches:

| Option Switch | Action | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`/active:no`** | Temporarily disables the user account. | `net user coder /active:no` |
| **`/expires:08/31/2026`** | Sets an account expiration date (or `/expires:never`). | `net user coder /expires:08/31/2026` |
| **`/passwordreq:yes`** | Requires the user to have a password. | `net user coder /passwordreq:yes` |
| **`/times:M-F,8am-5pm`** | Restricts login hours (e.g. only Monday-Friday, 8 AM to 5 PM). | `net user coder /times:M-F,8am-5pm` |

🗑️ Deleting a User

net user coder /delete


---

👑 Assigning Permissions with `net localgroup`

Creating a user only grants standard user permissions. To elevate a user to a local administrator (giving them UAC elevation privileges), add them to the local **Administrators** group:

* **Add to Administrators Group:**
  
  net localgroup Administrators coder /add
  
* **List Local Groups:** Running **`net localgroup`** without arguments lists all security groups (e.g. Administrators, Users, Guests).
* **Remove from a Group:**
  
  net localgroup Administrators coder /delete
  

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Elevation Required:**
> All user account creation (`net user /add`) and group modification (`net localgroup /add`) commands require **elevated administrator privileges** (UAC elevation). If run in a standard prompt, they fail with `System error 5 has occurred. Access is denied.`

> 👥 **Developer Joke:** Why did the local user account cross the Command Prompt? To get admin permission on the other side! 🚧

Chapter 12: Remote Access

🔌 Power Operations & Shutdown Controls

Managing 🪟 Windows 11 system states remotely or locally is handled by the **`shutdown`** command. This utility allows you to configure precise power-off actions:

* **`shutdown /s`**: Shuts down the computer.
* **`shutdown /r`**: Restarts the computer.
* **`shutdown /t [seconds]`**: Sets a delay timer before the action runs (e.g. `/t 120` delays the shutdown by 2 minutes).
* **`shutdown /f`**: Forces running applications to close without warning, preventing files from blocking the shutdown process.
* **`shutdown /a`**: Aborts and cancels any active, pending shutdown or restart timer.

Controlling a Remote Device:
If you have administrative credentials, you can target another computer on your network using the `/m` switch:

shutdown /s /m \\office-pc-02 /t 60 /f

*This forces a shutdown of the remote computer `office-pc-02` in 60 seconds.*

---

📶 Remote Shell Execution: WinRM & WinRS

To run interactive terminal tools on remote computers across a local area network, 🪟 Windows uses the built-in **Windows Remote Management (WinRM)** and **Windows Remote Shell (WinRS)** utilities.

1. Enabling WinRM Services (`winrm`)
Before you can connect to a computer remotely, the target machine must have the WinRM listener active. Open an elevated Command Prompt on the *target computer* and run:

winrm quickconfig

*This command automatically starts the WinRM service, configures it to launch on system boot, and opens required ports in the Windows Defender Firewall.*

2. Running Remote Commands (`winrs`)
Once WinRM is active on the remote computer, you can run commands on it from your *local computer* using `winrs`:
* **Check Remote Network Adapter Info:**
  
  winrs -r:office-pc-02 ipconfig
  
  *This executes the ipconfig command on `office-pc-02` and streams the text output back to your local command prompt window.*
* **Specifying Credentials:**
  If your current local user account does not have admin permissions on the target computer, supply credentials inline:
  
  winrs -r:office-pc-02 -u:Administrator -p:SecretPass123 ver

title: Chapter 13: Batch Files
content:
Chapter 13: Batch Files

📄 Shell Scripting Automation

A **batch file** (saved with the **`.bat`** extension) is an executable script containing a list of Command Prompt instructions. When you execute a batch file, the command interpreter executes the lines sequentially.

---

🛠️ Core Scripting Instructions

To write clean, interactive automation scripts in 🪟 Windows 11, developers use these standard commands:

1. Echoing Control (`@echo off`)
By default, the terminal prints every command line in the batch script before running it.
* **`@echo off`**: Add this at the absolute top of your script to hide command prompts from showing, making the terminal output look extremely clean.
* **`echo Message`**: Prints a custom message line to the console screen.

2. Pausing Execution (`pause`)
Temporarily freezes script execution and displays the text: `Press any key to continue . . .`. It waits for the user to press a key before moving to the next line. (Crucial for preventing the terminal window from auto-closing before you can read the output!).

3. Remarks and Comments (`rem` or `::`)
Used to write notes for developers that the computer ignores when running:

rem This is a standard remark comment
:: This is a shorthand modern comment


---

🔄 Branching, User Inputs, & Conditionals


graph TD
    start["Start Script"] --> input["set /p choice= (Yes/No)"]
    input --> cond{"Is choice Y?"}
    cond -- Yes --> labelY[":proceed"]
    cond -- No --> labelN[":abort"]
    labelY --> endS["End Script"]
    labelN --> endS
    
    style start fill:#1e293b,stroke:#3b82f6,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff
    style cond fill:#1e293b,stroke:#eab308,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff


1. User Prompts (`set /p`)
Prompts the user for a text string and saves it into a variable:

set /p folderName=Enter new folder name: 
mkdir %folderName%

*(Notice we wrap the variable name in `%` signs to read its value).*

2. Interactive Selection (`choice`)
Restricts the user's input to specific keys, returning an error level indicator depending on what was selected:

choice /c YN /m "Do you want to run the backup now?"

*Outputs: `Do you want to run the backup now? [Y,N]?`*

3. Conditional Checks (`if`)
Executes blocks based on filesystem states or string evaluations:
* **Check if file exists:**
  
  if exist config.txt (
      echo Configuration loaded!
  ) else (
      echo Warning: Configuration missing!
  )
  
* **Variable comparison:**
  
  if "%choice%"=="Y" goto proceed
  

4. Jump Labels (`goto`)
Directs script execution to jump to a specific label starting with a colon (`:`):

@echo off
set /p ans=Build app? (Y/N): 
if "%ans%"=="Y" goto build
if "%ans%"=="N" goto end

:build
echo Building Web App...
npm run build
pause

:end
echo Exiting script...

title: Chapter 14: Task Management
content:
Chapter 14: Task Management

📊 Process Auditing with `tasklist`

If an application freezes, hangs, or consumes too much CPU or RAM, system administrators use Command Line tools instead of the graphical Task Manager in 🪟 Windows 11:

* **List Processes:** Running **`tasklist`** displays a table of all active applications and background services, including their **Image Name**, Process ID (**PID**), Session Name, and **Mem Usage** (in KB).
* **Verbose Details (`/v`):**
  
  tasklist /v
  
  *Displays additional fields including the user account running each process and the exact window title name (e.g. `Nextsem - Google Chrome`).*
* **Filtering Results (`/fi`):**
  You can filter processes using query operators (like `gt` for greater than):
  
  tasklist /fi "memusage gt 100000"
  
  *Lists only the processes that consume more than 100 MB of system RAM.*

---

🪓 Terminating Tasks with `taskkill`

When a process becomes unresponsive, the **`taskkill`** utility forces it to close:

1. Kill by Process ID (`/pid`)
Every running process is assigned a unique numeric **PID** on boot. To terminate a specific instance:

taskkill /pid 4902 /f

*(The `/f` switch forces the process to close instantly without prompting the user to save work).*

2. Kill by Image Name (`/im`)
If you want to close all instances of an application (like closing all open Notepad windows):

taskkill /im notepad.exe /f


3. Tree Kill (`/t`)
Some applications launch multiple sub-processes (child processes). To close a parent process and all of its child processes recursively, use the `/t` switch:

taskkill /im chrome.exe /f /t

*This terminates Google Chrome and all of its active tabs and extensions at once.*

title: P0.5: Chrome DevTools & Debugging
content:
P0.5: Chrome DevTools & Debugging Google Chrome is more than just a browser—for web developers, it is the primary debugging environment. **Chrome DevTools** is a suite of web authoring and debugging tools built directly into the browser. This guide will take you from a DevTools newbie to an expert, covering layout inspection, advanced console hacks, JavaScript debugging with conditional breakpoints, and keyboard shortcuts. --- 👁️ Developer Profile --- 🛠️ Interactive DevTools Sandbox Below is a live, simulated Chrome DevTools environment. Use it to practice inspecting HTML styles, running console tables/timers, setting breakpoints, network throttling, and modifying application local storage: --- 1. Navigating the Panels To open Chrome DevTools, right-click any element on a webpage and select **Inspect**, or press **F12** (Windows/Linux) / **Cmd+Option+I** (Mac).
🖥️ Elements
Inspect and live-edit HTML tags, CSS rules, margins, and responsiveness.
💻 Console
Read logged outputs, view errors, and run arbitrary JavaScript expressions.
⚙️ Sources
Set breakpoints, step through JavaScript code execution line-by-line.
📡 Network
Track HTTP requests, inspect responses, payloads, and throttle speeds.
💾 Application
Audit LocalStorage, SessionStorage, cookies, and local database storage.
--- 2. Elements Panel Secrets The Elements panel is where you inspect layouts, typography, alignments, and colors.

🎨 Live Editing HTML & CSS

Double-click any HTML tag or attribute in the Elements tree to edit it live in the browser. You can click on any CSS rule in the Styles pane to change font-sizes, margins, or colors. These changes are temporary, making it perfect for rapid prototyping!

🖱️ Forcing Pseudo-states (:hover, :active)

Inspecting dropdown menus or hover tooltips is difficult because moving your mouse hides the item. In the Styles pane, click the :hov button and check the :hover or :active checkbox. DevTools freezes the element in that state permanently!

--- 3. Console Power-User Hacks While `console.log()` is useful, Chrome DevTools supports more powerful output formats:
📊 console.table()

Renders an array of objects into a beautiful, sortable table instead of nested dropdowns:

const students = [ { name: "Aman", role: "Frontend", level: 1 }, { name: "Rahul", role: "Backend", level: 2 } ]; console.table(students);
📁 console.group()

Organizes related logs together under collapsible segments:

console.group("User Details"); console.log("Name: Manoj"); console.log("Status: Certified"); console.groupEnd();
⏱️ console.time() & console.timeEnd()

Accurately measures execution speed for benchmarking database fetches or loop functions:

console.time("DB Fetch"); // Run complex task... console.timeEnd("DB Fetch"); // Outputs: DB Fetch: 1.45ms

The average salary of a frontend developer rises exponentially as they build experience and practical project portfolios. --- --- 3. Anatomy of an HTML5 Document HTML files are simply text documents. To describe the structure of a webpage, we add code (called **tags**) to the words we want to appear on the page. Tags act as containers that tell the browser how to interpret the content within them. Every HTML page requires a fundamental skeleton to function properly. My First Web Page

Breakdown of Key Elements: * ``: The DOCTYPE declaration tells the browser which version of HTML the page is using (HTML5). Text Formatting & Typography HTML provides specific tags to give structural and semantic meaning to text. Headings Headings range from `<h1>` to `<h6>`. Bold vs. Strong & Italic vs. Emphasis * `<b>`: Renders text in bold (presentation style only, implies no extra importance). * `<strong>`: Indicates text of strong importance (semantic markup, highly recommended). * `<i>`: Renders text in italics (presentation style only, e.g. for foreign words or technical terms). * `<em>`: Indicates emphasized text that subtly changes the meaning of a sentence (semantic markup). <p>This is a <strong>very important</strong> warning.</p> <p>I <em>think</em> Ivy was the first.</p> Superscript & Subscript * `<sup>`: Formats text as superscript (e.g., date suffixes like 4<sup>th</sup> or math exponents like E=MC<sup>2</sup>). * `<sub>`: Formats text as subscript (e.g., chemical formulas like H<sub>2</sub>O or footnotes). --- 5. White Space Collapsing When a browser encounters two or more consecutive spaces in the code, or a line break, it collapses them into a single space. This is known as **white space collapsing**. Semantic Markup & Annotations Semantic tags add metadata details to the page that are useful for search engines, screen readers, and translation tools. Quotations * `<blockquote>`: Used for longer, block-level quotations. It should always contain a `<p>` tag inside it. Milne said, <q>Some people talk to animals. Not many listen though.</q></p> Abbreviations & Acronyms * `<abbr>`: Used for abbreviations and acronyms. Use the `title` attribute to specify the full term. When hovered, the browser displays the full term as a tooltip. <p>The <abbr title="World Wide Web Consortium">W3C</abbr> sets web standards.</p> Citations & Definitions * `<cite>`: Used to reference a piece of work like a book, film, paper, or song (renders in italics). * `<dfn>`: Used for the defining instance of a new term. <p><cite>A Brief History of Time</cite> was written by Stephen Hawking.</p> <p>A <dfn>black hole</dfn> is a region of space from which nothing can escape.</p> Author Details & Content Updates * `<address>`: Used to contain contact details for the author of a page (renders in italics). * `<ins>`: Represents text that has been inserted into the document (usually rendered with an underline). * `<del>`: Represents text that has been deleted from the document (usually rendered with a line through it). * `<s>`: Indicates content that is no longer accurate or relevant (renders with a strikethrough). <address> <p><a href="mailto:support@nextsem.online">support@nextsem.online</a></p> </address> <p>It was the <del>worst</del> <ins>best</ins> idea I ever had.</p> <p><s>Was ₹999</s> Now Free!</p> --- 🎓 Lesson Assignment: Your First HTML Sandbox Create a file named `blog.html` and structure a tech blog post using headings, paragraphs, bold/italic, superscript, subscript, abbreviations, and citations. title: P2.1: CSS Selectors & Rules
content:
P2.1: CSS Selectors & Rules CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) brings your structural HTML webpages to life. In this lesson, we will master how to declare styles and target elements using selectors and cascading rules. --- 1. How CSS Works CSS works by associating rules with HTML elements. A CSS rule contains two main parts: a **selector** (which points to the HTML elements to style) and a **declaration** (which contains styling properties and values). /* Selector */ h1 { /* Property : Value */ font-family: Arial; color: #4ade80; } * **Property:** The visual aspect you want to change (e.g. `color`, `font-size`, `border`). * **Value:** The setting for that property (e.g. `red`, `12px`, `solid`). * Declarations are enclosed in curly brackets `{ }` and must end with a semicolon `;`. --- 2. Dynamic Styling Engagement Clean, modular CSS stylesheets decouple presentation logic from document structure, improving code maintainability. --- --- 3. Applying CSS to Webpages You can add CSS rules to your HTML in three different ways: External CSS (Recommended) Places all CSS rules in a separate file (e.g., `styles.css`) and links to it in the HTML ``. This separates content from presentation and allows multiple pages to share the same stylesheet. Internal CSS Places CSS rules directly inside a ` Inline CSS Applies styles directly to individual tags using the `style` attribute. > [!WARNING] > Inline styles should generally be avoided because they blend content and presentation, making it harder to maintain styling across large websites.

This is inline styled text.

--- 4. CSS Selectors Reference Selectors tell the browser which HTML elements a rule applies to. You can target elements based on their type, nesting, or attributes. | Selector Type | Syntax | Meaning | Example | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Universal** | `*` | Targets all elements on the page. | `* { margin: 0; }` | | **Type** | `h1, p` | Matches HTML element names. | `p { line-height: 1.5; }` | | **Class** | `.note` | Matches elements with the specified class. | `.note { color: gray; }` | | **ID** | `#intro` | Matches the unique element with the specified `id`. | `#intro { font-weight: bold; }` | | **Child** | `li > a` | Matches direct children of a parent element. | `li > a { color: blue; }` | | **Descendant** | `p a` | Matches nested elements, regardless of depth. | `p a { text-decoration: none; }` | | **Adjacent Sibling** | `h1 + p` | Matches the first sibling immediately after an element. | `h1 + p { margin-top: 10px; }` | | **General Sibling** | `h1 ~ p` | Matches any sibling element that follows. | `h1 ~ p { color: slate; }` | --- 5. CSS Cascade & Specificity When multiple rules target the same element, browsers resolve conflicts using **the cascade**, which determines precedence based on three principles: 1. Last Rule If two selectors are identical in specificity and target the same element, the rule that appears **last** in the stylesheet overrides previous ones. i { color: green; } i { color: red; } /* Wins! text will be red */ 2. Specificity More specific selectors override more general selectors. Specificity is calculated using a scoring system: * Inline style = 1000 * ID selector = 100 * Class / Attribute selector = 10 * Type selector (HTML tag) = 1 * Universal selector = 0 p { color: white; } /* Specificity: 1 */ .note { color: gray; } /* Specificity: 10 (Wins!) */ p#intro { color: green; } /* Specificity: 101 (Wins over class!) */ 3. The `!important` Flag You can write `!important` after any property value to override all specificity and ordering calculations. Use this flag sparingly, as it makes debugging layout rules extremely difficult. p { color: red !important; } /* Overrides all specific classes or IDs */ --- 6. CSS Inheritance Some CSS properties are **inherited** by child elements. For example, if you set `font-family` or `color` on the `` element, all paragraphs and headings inside the body will inherit that font and color automatically. However, layout-based properties (like `background-color`, `border`, `margin`, and `padding`) are **not inherited** to prevent visual clutter. The `inherit` Keyword: You can force any property to inherit a value from its parent by using the `inherit` value: .page { /* Inherits padding dimensions set on parent */ padding: inherit; } --- 🎓 Practice Assignment 1. Create a page `selectors.html` and a stylesheet `styles.css`. Link them using an external link. 2. Build an unordered list where some links (``) are nested inside `
  • ` elements. 3. Write CSS rules using Type, Class, ID, Child (`li > a`), and Adjacent Sibling (`h1 + p`) selectors. 4. Test specificity by adding conflict rules for the same paragraph, and verify which color wins in Chrome.

3. CSS Color Formats

Every color on a screen is created by mixing red, green, and blue light (pixels). CSS supports several ways to specify these values:

1. Color Names
CSS recognizes 147 predefined color names (e.g. `DarkCyan`, `silver`, `white`, `black`, `tomato`). Their usage is limited because they do not cover custom design system values.

2. Hex Codes
The most common web format. Renders as a pound sign `#` followed by six hexadecimal digits (each pair representing Red, Green, and Blue from `00` to `ff`).

h1 { color: #4ade80; } /* Neon Green */


3. RGB Values
Specifies color intensity as numbers between `0` and `255` (representing Red, Green, Blue).

h1 { color: rgb(74, 222, 128); }


4. HSL Values (Recommended for systems)
An intuitive format based on human color perception:
* **Hue:** The color itself, expressed as an angle on the color wheel (0 to 360). Red is 0/360, Green is 120, Blue is 240.
* **Saturation:** The amount of gray in the color (0% is completely gray/monochrome, 100% is full color saturation).
* **Lightness:** Renders the brightness/luminosity (0% is solid black, 100% is solid white, 50% is normal).


h1 { color: hsl(120, 70%, 50%); }


---

4. Transparency & Opacity

CSS provides two distinct ways to make elements transparent: the `opacity` property and **alpha channels**.

The `opacity` Property
Specifies transparency for the **entire element**, including its text and any nested child elements. The value ranges from `0.0` (fully transparent) to `1.0` (fully opaque).

.card {
  opacity: 0.5; /* Renders card background, borders, and TEXT at 50% opacity */
}


Alpha Transparency (RGBA / HSLA)
Sets transparency for **only the specific property** it is applied to (e.g., just the background color), leaving the nested child elements (like text) fully opaque and readable. 

* `rgba(red, green, blue, alpha)`
* `hsla(hue, saturation, lightness, alpha)`
* *Alpha:* Ranges from `0.0` (invisible) to `1.0` (opaque).


.card {
  /* Renders a semi-transparent background, but text remains solid and readable! */
  background-color: rgba(15, 23, 42, 0.5); 
}


---

5. Accessibility & Contrast

When choosing foreground and background colors, it is crucial to ensure there is enough contrast for the text to be readable. 

* **Low Contrast:** Hard to read, especially in bright sunlight or for users with visual impairments.
* **High Contrast:** Renders crisp readability.
* **Medium Contrast:** For long spans of body text, slightly reducing contrast (e.g., off-white text on dark slate) reduces eye strain.

> [!TIP]
> **Typography Tip:** If you reverse text (light text on a dark background), increase the line height (`line-height`) and font weight (`font-weight`) slightly. This counteracts the visual blending of glowing white text against black.

---

content:
P2.3: Resilient CSS Box Model Every element on a webpage is treated as a rectangular box. In this lesson, we will master the box model rules that control spacing, borders, shadows, and visibility. --- 1. Box Model Components Every HTML box is made up of four layers, nesting from the inside out: ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ MARGIN │ │ ┌───────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ BORDER │ │ │ │ ┌───────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ │ │ PADDING │ │ │ │ │ │ ┌───────────────────┐ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ CONTENT AREA │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └───────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ └───────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ └───────────────────────────────────┘ │ └───────────────────────────────────────────┘ 1. **Content Area:** The actual text, images, or child elements (sized via `width` and `height`). 2. **Padding:** The space between the content and the border. Padding inherits the background color of the element. 3. **Border:** A line surrounding the padding and content. 4. **Margin:** The empty space outside the border that separates this box from adjacent boxes. Margins are always transparent. .card { width: 300px; padding: 20px; border: 1px solid #334155; margin: 15px; } --- 2. Layout & Box Model Metrics Mastering padding and margin scaling is crucial for achieving professional spacing alignments in user interfaces. --- --- 3. Box Dimensions & Overflow Sizing Limits You can define exact dimensions or set flexible limits to prevent layouts from breaking: * `min-width` / `max-width`: Limits how narrow or wide a box can scale. * `min-height` / `max-height`: Limits how short or tall a box can scale. Overflow Control (`overflow`) If a box has fixed dimensions and its content is too large to fit, the `overflow` property controls the behavior: * `hidden`: Crops the overflowing content (renders it invisible). * `scroll`: Adds horizontal and vertical scrollbars, even if the content fits. * `auto`: Adds scrollbars only if the content overflows the box. .scroll-box { height: 200px; overflow: auto; } --- 4. Spacing, Borders, and Shorthands Padding & Margin Shorthand You can declare padding and margins for each side individually (`padding-top`, `padding-right`, `padding-bottom`, `padding-left`) or use a shorthand sequence following a **clockwise order (Top, Right, Bottom, Left)**: /* Clockwise: Top=10px, Right=20px, Bottom=10px, Left=20px */ padding: 10px 20px 10px 20px; /* Symmetrical: Top/Bottom=10px, Left/Right=20px */ padding: 10px 20px; /* Uniform: All 4 sides get 15px */ padding: 15px; Collapsing Margins When the bottom margin of one element touches the top margin of another, they collapse into a single margin. The browser does not add them together; instead, it renders only the larger of the two margins. Centering Block Elements To center a block box inside its parent container, specify a fixed `width` and set the left and right margins to `auto`: .centered-container { width: 90%; max-width: 1200px; margin: 0 auto; /* Top/Bottom=0, Left/Right automatically balanced */ } Border Shorthand Sets width, style, and color in a single declaration: /* border: width style color; */ border: 3px dotted #4ade80; * **Styles:** `solid`, `dotted`, `dashed`, `double`, `groove`, `ridge`, `inset`, `outset`, `none`. --- 5. CSS3 Rounded Corners & Shadows Border Radius (`border-radius`) Creates rounded corners on any box. Value can be in pixels or percentages (50% on a square box creates a perfect circle). .rounded-card { border-radius: 12px; } .profile-avatar { width: 80px; height: 80px; border-radius: 50%; } Box Shadows (`box-shadow`) Adds a drop shadow around the element box: /* box-shadow: horizontal-offset vertical-offset blur-radius spread-radius color; */ box-shadow: 0px 4px 20px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.3); * Add `inset` at the start to render the shadow inside the box borders. --- 6. Display & Visibility Properties The `display` property determines how an element behaves in the document flow: * `block`: Starts on a new line and stretches to fill the full width of its parent (e.g. `
`, `

`, `

`). * `inline`: Flows inline with text. Ignores width and height properties (e.g. ``, ``, ``). * `inline-block`: Flows inline like a span, but respects width, height, margins, and padding. * `none`: Completely hides the element and removes it from the page layout flow. Display `none` vs. Visibility `hidden` * `display: none`: Hides the box completely. Adjacent elements shift to fill the empty space. * `visibility: hidden`: Hides the content of the box, but leaves the physical box in the layout (renders as a blank gap). --- 🎓 Practice Assignment 1. Create a page `box.html` and a stylesheet `styles.css`. 2. Construct a card container (`

What is JSX? **JSX** is a syntax extension for JavaScript that looks like HTML, but compiles down to standard JavaScript function calls. Hello World

JSX Syntax Rules To write valid JSX, you must follow three strict rules: Rule 1: Always Return a Single Root Element JSX elements must be wrapped in a single parent tag (like a `
` or a React Fragment `<>...`). // ❌ INVALID return (

Welcome

To React

); Rule 2: Close All Tags All tags must be explicitly closed, including self-closing tags like ``, `

Instead of modifying the real browser DOM directly (which is slow), React follows a three-step process: 1. **Virtual Copy**: When state changes, React creates a new virtual representation of the entire UI page in memory. 2. **Diffing Algorithm**: React compares the new Virtual DOM with the previous snapshot to identify exactly which elements changed. 3. **Reconciliation (Patching)**: React updates *only* those specific modified nodes in the real browser DOM. --- --- 🎓 Practice Assignment 1. Build a component with a text input field and a "Clear" button. 2. Clicking "Clear" should empty the input field's value directly and immediately focus the input field using `useRef`. 3. title: P4.7: React Routing
content:
P4.7: React Routing In traditional websites, navigating between pages requires the browser to reload the entire HTML page. Modern React applications are built as **Single Page Applications (SPAs)**. They load the page once, and then swap out components dynamically when the URL changes. To handle page transitions without reloading the page, we use a routing library like **React Router** or **Next.js Routing**. --- 1. Traditional vs Client-Side Routing * **Traditional Routing**: User clicks link -> Browser requests new page -> Server returns HTML -> Full page refresh (slow, white flash). * **Client-Side Routing**: User clicks link -> React intercept click -> Updates the URL -> Swaps out matching component dynamically (instant, smooth). --- 2. Using React Router Components React Router provides three core components to handle client-side routing: 1. `BrowserRouter` Wraps your entire application to enable URL tracking. 2. `Routes` & `Route` Defines the mapping between URL paths and React components. import { BrowserRouter, Routes, Route } from 'react-router-dom'; import Home from './Home'; import About from './About'; function App() { return ( } /> } /> ); } 3. `Link` instead of `` Always use the `` component for internal navigation. Standard `` anchor tags will trigger a full browser page reload, defeating the purpose of an SPA! import { Link } from 'react-router-dom'; // ❌ WRONG (Triggers full reload) About Us // RIGHT (Client-side routing) About Us --- 3. Reading Dynamic Parameters You can capture values from the URL (like user IDs or chapter names) by declaring a wildcard path: // Route mapping } /> Inside the component, use the `useParams` Hook to read the value: import { useParams } from 'react-router-dom'; function UserProfile() { const { userId } = useParams(); return
Loading profile for user #{userId}...
; } --- --- 🎓 Practice Assignment 1. Set up a basic React app structure with two views: `Home` and `Dashboard`. 2. Configure a router using `Routes` and navigation layout links. 3. Verify in your browser devtools that clicking navigation links updates the URL without triggering a full page reload.

title: P4.8: Context API
content:
P4.8: Context API As React applications grow, passing props down through multiple layers of components can become exhausting. This problem is known as **Prop Drilling**. To solve this, React provides the **Context API**, which acts as a global broadcast system, allowing components to share data directly without passing props through intermediate elements. --- 1. The Prop Drilling Problem Imagine you have a `Theme` state declared in `App`. The `App` nests a `MainLayout`, which nests a `Sidebar`, which nests a `ThemeSelectorButton`. To get the theme values to the button, you must pass the props down through every single layout container, even if they don't use it! [App State: theme] └─► [MainLayout] (no-op pass-through) └─► [Sidebar] (no-op pass-through) └─► [ThemeSelectorButton] (uses theme) With **Context**, the button can request the theme data directly from the root provider, skipping the intermediate components entirely: [App Provider: theme] ═══════════════(broadcast)═══════════════► [ThemeSelectorButton] --- 2. Setting Up Context: 3 Simple Steps Let's build a global Theme Context step-by-step: Step 1: Create the Context Create a new file `ThemeContext.js` and call `createContext()`. import { createContext } from 'react'; export const ThemeContext = createContext("dark"); // Default value is "dark" Step 2: Provide the Context Wrap your top-level components inside the Context `Provider` tag and pass the state value inside the `value` prop. import React, { useState } from 'react'; import { ThemeContext } from './ThemeContext'; import MainLayout from './MainLayout'; export default function App() { const [theme, setTheme] = useState("dark"); return ( ); } Step 3: Consume the Context Inside any child component, use the `useContext` Hook to read the value directly. import React, { useContext } from 'react'; import { ThemeContext } from './ThemeContext'; export default function ThemeSelectorButton() { // Read value directly from global broadcast const theme = useContext(ThemeContext); return (
Current Theme is: {theme}
); } --- 3. Comparing Local vs Global State Adoption For local concerns (like toggle states, form inputs), keep using `useState`. For global concerns (user authentication, active themes, shopping cart items), adopt the Context API. --- --- 🎓 Practice Assignment 1. Create a `UserContext` that stores a user profile object `{ name: "Guest", isLoggedIn: false }`. 2. Wrap your application inside the provider and implement a button that sets `isLoggedIn: true`. 3. In a nested header component, dynamically display the user's name if logged in, or a "Sign In" button if guest.

title: P5.1: Node.js & Express Basics
content:
P5.1: Node.js & Express Basics

Until now, we have written JavaScript code that runs exclusively inside the browser DOM. **Node.js** allows us to run JavaScript on our local computer or backend servers, opening the door to full-stack development!

---

1. What is Node.js?

**Node.js** is an open-source, cross-platform JavaScript runtime environment built on Google Chrome's V8 engine. It executes JavaScript code outside of a web browser.

Key Characteristics:
* **Asynchronous and Event-Driven**: Node.js uses a single-threaded event loop to handle thousands of concurrent requests without blocking operations.
* **No Browser APIs**: Since Node.js runs on a server, there is no `window`, `document`, or `alert()`. Instead, you gain access to server APIs like `fs` (File System) and `path`.

---

2. Package Management with NPM

**NPM** (Node Package Manager) is the default package manager for Node.js. It allows you to download and manage third-party libraries (packages) for your project.

To start a new Node.js project, run this command in your terminal:

npm init -y

This generates a `package.json` file, which tracks your project's dependencies and configuration metadata.

---

3. Creating a Server with Express

**Express** is a minimal and flexible web application framework for Node.js, providing a robust set of features for building web servers and APIs.

Step 1: Install Express
Run the install command in your project folder:

npm install express


Step 2: Write your server script (`server.js`)
Create a file named `server.js` and write the setup:


const express = require('express');
const app = express();
const PORT = 5000;

// Define a simple root route
app.get('/', (req, res) => {
  res.send('Hello from the Node.js Server!');
});

// Start the server listening on PORT
app.listen(PORT, () => {
  console.log(`Server is running at http://localhost:${PORT}`);
});


Step 3: Run your server
Start the script in your terminal:

node server.js

Open `http://localhost:5000` in your web browser, and you will see your server response!

---

4. Node.js Event Loop Performance

The Node.js event loop handles operations asynchronously, making it highly efficient for I/O-intensive web servers.

P5.4: Backend Deployment

Your local Express server is ready! Now we must deploy it to the cloud so that users around the world can access your API. 

In this final phase lesson, we will secure our configurations using environment variables, handle cross-origin constraints, and deploy our server.

---

1. Environment Variables (`.env`)

You must never commit secret credentials (like database passwords, API keys) directly into your git repository. Instead, store them in a local `.env` file and read them using `dotenv`.

Step 1: Install dotenv

npm install dotenv


Step 2: Create a `.env` file (Add to `.gitignore`!)

PORT=5000
MONGODB_URI=mongodb+srv://admin:my-secret-password@cluster.mongodb.net/db


Step 3: Load env variables in your server code

require('dotenv').config();

const port = process.env.PORT || 5000;
const dbUri = process.env.MONGODB_URI;


---

2. Managing CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)

By default, web browsers block frontend code (e.g. running on `http://localhost:3000`) from requesting resources from a backend API running on a different domain (e.g. `http://localhost:5000`). This is a security constraint called **CORS**.

To allow your frontend to query your backend API, install and configure the `cors` middleware:


npm install cors



const express = require('express');
const cors = require('cors');
const app = express();

// Enable CORS for all incoming requests
app.use(cors());

// Or limit to your frontend domain:
app.use(cors({
  origin: 'https://nextsem.online'
}));


---

3. Deployment Platforms

You can host Express backend APIs on several popular cloud hosting platforms:

* **Render (Recommended)**: Free tier, easy Git integration, auto-builds.
* **Railway**: Quick deployments, great database support.
* **Fly.io**: Fast global container-based server hosting.

Step-by-Step Render Deployment Guide:
1. Push your backend code repository to GitHub (ensure `.env` is *not* pushed).
2. Create an account on [Render.com](https://render.com).
3. Select **New** -> **Web Service** -> Link your GitHub repository.
4. Set the **Start Command** to `node server.js` or `npm start`.
5. Go to the **Environment** settings tab and enter your production `MONGODB_URI` and `PORT` values.
6. Click **Deploy Web Service**. Render will build and host your API live!

---

4. Full-Stack Data Flow

Once deployed, your frontend uses JavaScript `fetch` to request data from your live backend URL, completing the full-stack loop:


┌──────────────────┐               Request (fetch API)               ┌──────────────────┐
│  React Frontend  │ ══════════════════════════════════════════════► │  Express Server  │
│  (Next.js App)   │ ◄────────────────────────────────────────────── │  (Render Cloud)  │
└──────────────────┘               Response (JSON data)              └──────────────────┘

P7.1: Technical Mock Interviews

Landing a software engineering role requires more than coding skills. You must be able to explain your technical decisions clearly under interview pressure.

In this lesson, we will cover the core JavaScript, React, and browser networking questions that recur in technical mock interviews.

---

1. Core JavaScript Conceptual Questions

Question 1: What is a Closure in JavaScript?
A closure is the combination of a function bundled together with references to its surrounding state (the lexical environment). In other words, a closure gives an inner function access to the outer function's scope even after the outer function has returned.


function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0; // Lexical scope variable
  return function() {
    count++; // Accesses parent variable
    return count;
  };
}

const counter = makeCounter();
console.log(counter()); // 1
console.log(counter()); // 2


Question 2: What is the Event Loop?
JavaScript is single-threaded. The **Event Loop** is the mechanism that allows JavaScript to perform non-blocking operations by offloading tasks (like timers, network requests) to the browser web APIs, and then pushing callback functions onto the call stack when the stack is empty.

---

2. React Core Interview Focus

Question: What is the difference between state and props?
* **Props**: Configuration parameters passed down from a parent component. They are read-only (immutable) and cannot be modified by the component that receives them.
* **State**: Local data storage managed within the component itself. State changes trigger component re-rendering and are mutable via the setter function (`setState` / `useState`).

---

3. High-Frequency Interview Practice Sheet

Make sure you can comfortably explain the following concepts:
* **CSS Specificity**: How the browser decides which styles to apply based on selectors types (IDs > Classes > Tags).
* **Promise vs Async/Await**: Syntactic differences in handling asynchronous JavaScript.
* **CORS Errors**: Why browsers block cross-origin requests and how CORS headers resolve it.

title: P7.2: ATS Resume Writing

P7.2: ATS Resume Writing

Most tech companies use **Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS)** to filter resumes before a human recruiter ever sees them. If your resume is not formatted to be easily readable by these bots, you will be automatically rejected.

In this lesson, we will restructure your resume using standard single-column formats and impact-driven action formulas.

---

1. ATS Layout Rules

To ensure tracking systems parse your resume text correctly:
* **Single Column Only**: Avoid two-column layouts, tables, grids, text boxes, and sidebars. Bots read text top-to-bottom and left-to-right, and columns confuse them.
* **Standard Fonts**: Use clean, web-safe sans-serif fonts (like Arial, Calibri, or Inter).
* **Text Format**: Avoid saving your resume as an image. Always export it as a clean PDF or Docx containing selectable text.
* **No icons/graphics**: Remove stars, meters, and progress bars showing "skill percentages". These cannot be parsed by bots.

---

2. Writing Impact-Driven Bullet Points

Hiring managers want to see results, not just a list of responsibilities. Use the **Google XY-Z Formula** to write your project descriptions:

> **Google X-Y-Z Formula:**
> **Accomplished [X]**, as measured by **[Y]**, by doing **[Z]**

Examples:
* **❌ Poor**: "Responsible for writing Express APIs and connecting them to MongoDB."
* ** Good**: "Built a secure Express task API connected to MongoDB, decreasing query latency by **24%** through the implementation of database indexing."
* **❌ Poor**: "Made the dashboard layout responsive on mobile screens."
* ** Good**: "Redesigned the curriculum layout using responsive CSS Grid, reducing mobile bounce rate by **15%** and improving accessibility scores."

---
